Surah al-Talaq (Chapter 65)

It is also called "al-Nisa' al-Qusra" (the Shorter Surah of the Women). Thus Ibn Mas'ud named it, as al-Bukhari and others narrated. Al-Dawudi denied this, saying: "I do not consider 'al-Qusra' to be authentically transmitted, and nothing in the Qur'an is called 'qusra' or 'sughra'." Ibn Hajar responded to him, saying that this is a rejection of established reports without any basis, and that shortness and length are relative matters. Al-Bukhari has narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit that he said: "The longest of the two longs (tula al-tulayayn)," meaning Surah al-A'raf, which is Medinan by consensus.

The number of its verses differs: in the Basran reckoning it has eleven verses, and in all other reckonings twelve verses. When Allah, glorified is He, mentioned earlier, ﴿Indeed, among your spouses and your children are enemies to you﴾ [al-Taghabun: 14], and enmity may lead to divorce, He mentioned here divorce, and guided, exalted is He, to separation from them in a good manner. He, mighty and majestic is He, also mentioned what relates to children in general. So the Mighty One said:

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾: The address is specifically to the Prophet (ﷺ), while the ruling applies generally, because the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, is the leader of his nation. This is like saying to the chief and eldest of a people, "O so-and-so, do such-and-such," to show his precedence and to acknowledge his leadership, and that he speaks on their behalf, and that they proceed from his opinion and do not act independently of him in any matter. Thus he alone stands in for all of them in their rulings and takes the place of all of them. In this there is a demonstration of the exalted rank of his position, upon him be prayers and peace. For this reason the word "Prophet" was chosen, because it indicates the elevation of his station (ﷺ). It has also been said that the address is like the call directed to him (ﷺ), except that the plural pronoun was chosen for honour, like what is in the saying:

"Surely have mercy on me, O God of Muhammad."

It has also been said that after addressing him, upon him be prayers and peace, with the call, Allah, glorified is He, turned the address away from him to his nation, honouring him (ﷺ), because divorce is disliked, so he was not addressed with it out of reverence. Some scholars took the statement in this view to be with an implied verb: i.e., "Say to your nation: ﴿when you divorce﴾." It has also been said: the call to the nation was omitted, and the implied meaning is, "O Prophet and nation of the Prophet, when you divorce..." Whichever it is, the meaning is "when you intend to divorce them," treating one who is about to undertake an action as though he has already begun it. They agreed that without this figurative usage the sentence would not be sound, because it would involve obtaining what is already obtained, or the meaning would be "when you divorce, then divorce them again," which is not intended. Some researchers said: you may say there is no need for that; rather, it is the specific linked to the general, which is more eloquent in indicating necessity, as one says, "If you strike Zayd, then strike him a severe blow," because the meaning is: if a blow proceeds from you, let it be a severe one. This is better than interpreting it as intention. End of quote. You know that what is apparent in what he mentioned is that it also carries the meaning of intention.

﴿So divorce them for their waiting period﴾: i.e., at the onset of their waiting period. The lam indicates a time-point, as in "I wrote it for four nights remaining from Jumada al-Ula," or "they are beginning it," according to what al-Zamakhshari estimated. Abu Hayyan criticised this with what requires examination. The consideration of "beginning" is the view of one who holds that the waiting period is by menstruation, namely the qurū' in the verse of al-Baqarah, like the Imam Abu Hanifa, so that divorce occurs in the state of purity, which is the divorce commanded. The command to pronounce it in that state implies the prohibition of pronouncing it during menstruation.

All of them have stated that that divorce during menstruation is innovated and forbidden. The condition of purity was qualified by the woman not having been had sexually during it. This is derived, and the consideration of "beginning" is supported, by what was narrated by the two Imams Malik and al-Shafi'i, the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, and others, from Ibn Umar: that he divorced his wife while she was menstruating, and Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became angry about it, then said: "Let him take her back, then keep her until she becomes pure, then she menstruates and becomes pure again. Then if it occurs to him to divorce her, let him divorce her while she is pure before he touches her. That is the waiting period by which Allah commanded that women be divorced."

The Prophet (ﷺ) recited: "O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them at their waiting period." Ibn Umar, as Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from him, used to recite in this way, and so did Ibn Abbas. In another narration from both of them, they recited "for their waiting period" (li-qubuli 'iddatihinna). He who holds that the waiting period is by purities, namely the qurū', in that verse, like the Imam al-Shafi'i, attaches the lam of time to the verb and does not consider "beginning." It was objected to the interpretation "those about to begin their waiting period" that if what is meant is entering upon its first part, then this is al-Shafi'i's view, and it is not against him and against the opponent, but for him alone; and if what is meant is customary approach, then it contradicts the implication of the wording, because when the lam enters a time it conveys the meaning of fixing and specifying that time, not beginning it. As for the argument from the recitation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as contained in the previous hadith, that "qubul" of a thing is its first part, the opposite of its "dubur," these are confirming the school of al-Shafi'i, not refuting it. The waiting period being by purities is supported by the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: "li-qubuli tuhrihinna" (at the beginning of their purity). Some said the sense is "li-atha'ri 'iddatihinna" (at the purities of their waiting period). This was objected to: if the genitive construction is taken in the sense of "min" (from), it indicates that the qur' is both menstruation and purity together; and if it is taken in the sense of "li" (for), then what is in your saying "li-atharil-hayd" (for the purities of menstruation) suffices as a disagreeable and rejected reading, together with what it contains of an unfounded supposition.

In al-Kashshaf: the intended meaning of the verse is that they are divorced in a purity in which they have not been had sexually, and then left alone until their waiting period ends. This is the best kind of divorce, the most within the Sunnah, and the furthest from regret. What supports it is what is related from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i that the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to prefer that a man not divorce her for the Sunnah except with a single divorce, and then not pronounce anything else until the waiting period ends. It was more excellent in their view than that a man divorce three times in three purities. Malik said: "I do not know the divorce of the Sunnah except as one divorce," and he disliked three, whether together or separated. As for Abu Hanifa and his companions, they disliked only more than one divorce in a single purity; but separated across purities, no. This is because of what is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said to Ibn Umar when he divorced his wife while she was menstruating: "This is not what Allah commanded you. The Sunnah is that you await the purity, then divorce her at each qur' one pronouncement." It is also related that he, upon him be prayers and peace, said to Umar: "Order your son to take her back, then leave her until she menstruates and becomes pure, then let him divorce her if he wishes."

According to al-Shafi'i there is no harm in sending three together, and he said: "I do not know in the number of divorces any sunnah or innovation; it is permissible." Malik observes in the Sunnah divorce the one pronouncement and the time; Abu Hanifa observes separation and the time; al-Shafi'i observes the time only. End of quote.

In Fath al-Qadir, in the argument for the non-disliking of separating over purities and its being of the Sunnah-type divorce, there is a narration other than what was mentioned from Ibn Umar as well; he said what he said in it, except that in the end he preferred its acceptance. By "sending three at once" is meant what covers pronouncing them in several separate phrases, such as saying, "You are divorced, you are divorced, you are divorced," or with a single phrase, such as saying, "You are divorced three times." There is disagreement about whether this three-fold pronouncement takes effect, and likewise about whether divorce takes effect at all during menstruation. According to the Imamiyya, divorce does not take effect with the phrase of three, nor during menstruation, because it is a forbidden innovation. The Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "Whoever does an action that is not upon our command, it is rejected." This was transmitted by more than one person from Ibn al-Musayyab and a group of the Successors. Some people, among them, it is said, Tawus and Ikrimah, said: a triple divorce with one utterance takes effect as one. This was narrated by Abu Dawud from Ibn Abbas, and it is the choice of Ibn Taymiyya from the Hanbalis. In the Two Sahihs: Abu al-Sahba' said to Ibn Abbas: "Do you not know that three were counted as one during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, and the early part of Umar's caliphate?" He said: "Yes." In a narration of Muslim: Ibn Abbas said, "Divorce during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, and two years of Umar's caliphate was the divorce of three counted as one. Then Umar said: 'People have hastened in a matter in which they had time for deliberation, so if we enforce it upon them...' and he enforced it upon them." Among them some said, regarding a woman who has been consummated, three take effect; regarding one not consummated, one takes effect, citing what is in Muslim, Abu Dawud, and al-Nasa'i: "Abu al-Sahba' frequently questioned Ibn Abbas, and said: 'Do you not know that when a man divorced his wife three times before consummation, they counted it as one?' Ibn Abbas said: 'Yes. When a man divorced his wife three times before consummation, they counted that as one during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, and the early part of Umar's caliphate.'" The hadith. But what the majority of the Companions, the Successors, and those after them among the leading Muslim scholars held, including the four Imams, is that three take effect when pronounced at once. Indeed Imam Ibn al-Humam mentioned the occurrence of a silent consensus (ijma' sukuti) of the Companions on its taking effect.

It is related that most of their mujtahids, such as Ali, may Allah honour his face, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayra, Uthman ibn Affan, and Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-'As, gave explicit legal opinions to that effect. It is also mentioned that Umar's enforcement of the three upon them, without the Companions opposing him despite their knowledge that they had been one, can only be explained by their having become aware in a later period of the existence of an abrogating ruling (nasikh), or by their knowing that the ruling had ended, since they knew it was tied to meanings whose cessation they recognised in a later period. Ibn Hajar, in al-Tuhfa, favoured the answer of awareness of an abrogating ruling, after mentioning two other answers and refuting them. Soon, if God wills, some elevated (marfu') reports will be cited that are used as evidence for the occurrence of three. However, it has been said that the three in them may be with three phrases, such as "You are divorced, you are divorced, you are divorced," which is probably the apparent meaning, and not with a single phrase such as "You are divorced three times." In that case, this cannot serve to refute those who did not make three take effect with this formula. But when the consensus, even if silent, on its taking effect is valid, it is not fitting except to agree and remain silent. The interpretation of what was related from Umar is as such. For this reason some of the Imams said: if a judge rules that three pronounced at once count as one, his ruling is not enforced.

Because there is no room for independent legal reasoning (ijtihad) in it, given the consensus of the recognized Imams on this point, even though they differ over whether one who pronounces it in this manner commits a sin. Whoever holds that it is sinful relies on what al-Nasa'i narrated from Mahmud ibn Labid, who said: "We were informed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about a man who divorced his wife three times at once. He stood up angry and said: 'Is the Book of Allah being played with while I am still among you?!' until a man stood up and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall I not kill him?'" And on what 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated from 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, that his father divorced a wife of his a thousand times, so 'Ubadah set out and asked him (ﷺ), and the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "She has become irrevocably separated by three in disobedience to Allah, and nine hundred and ninety-seven remain as transgression and wrongdoing; if Allah wills, He will punish him, and if He wills, He will forgive him." From this it is understood that the prohibition extends also to pronouncing more than the permitted number. This is the apparent meaning of the words of Ibn al-Rif'ah, and what is implied by the statement of al-Ruyani, which al-Zarkashi and others relied upon, that the one who does it is to be disciplined (ta'zir). It was justified on the basis that he engaged in something like a corrupt contract, which is forbidden. This was disputed on grounds that are open to question, and by what is in the Sunan of Abu Dawud from Mujahid, who said: "I was with Ibn 'Abbas when a man came to him and said: 'He divorced his wife three times.' He said to him: 'You have disobeyed your Lord, and your wife has become separated from you,' and other such things."

Whoever holds that it is not sinful relies on what the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated: that 'Uwaymir al-'Ajlani, when he performed li'an with his wife, divorced her three times before the Prophet (ﷺ) informed him of her prohibition upon him. He said: "If it were sinful, he would have forbidden him from it, because he pronounced it believing that the marital bond still remained; and with the belief in its continuation, combining them is forbidden according to the opponent. And with the prohibition, it would be obligatory to reject it upon the scholar and to teach the ignorant, and neither of these occurred. This indicates that there is no prohibition." He also relies on the fact that a group of the Companions did it, among them 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, who divorced his wife Tumadir three times in her presence, and al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, who divorced his wife Shahbanu three times when she congratulated him on the caliphate after the death of 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face. Some of the Hanafis said regarding this that it is to be understood as meaning that they said "three" in accordance with the Sunnah. This is further from the truth than the view of some Shafi'is concerning the reports indicating sin in it, that it is to be understood as having occurred during menstruation, so the sin in it is from that aspect.

It has been argued that it is sinful when done during menstruation by what is even clearer than that, such as the two earlier narrations reported from al-Kashshaf. In using these two to establish the prohibition of sending the three together there is a point for discussion. It may perhaps be argued from the second for the obligation of taking her back, but some eminent Shafi'is have stated that it is not obligatory but recommended in an innovative (bid'i) divorce. The reason it is not obligatory is that a command to command something is not itself a command to that thing. And in (the narration) "let him take her back" there is no command to Ibn 'Umar, because it is a derivative of the command of 'Umar; so the meaning is "let him take her back" for the sake of your command, since you are his father. The derivation of recommendation from it in that case comes only from the context. When he takes her back, the sin connected with the wife's right is removed, but not the ruling on the marriage itself. Taking her back is a cutting off of the harm from its root, so it is like repentance, which removes the root of the sin. By this it is distinguished from burying spittle in the mosque, for that cuts off the continuation of the harm but not its root, since the defiling of the mosque has already taken place. What has been said is refuted by this: that the revocation of the return, as a prohibition, like repentance, indicates its obligation; for something's being treated as equivalent to an obligatory act in one of its particular respects does not require its obligation. Nor may one rely on what the verse requires by way of prohibiting divorce during menstruation to establish that divorce in it is invalid, since according to Abu Hanifah a prohibition does not necessarily entail invalidity in every case, while according to al-Shafi'i it indicates invalidity in acts of worship and in transactions when it refers to the contract itself, or to something within it or inseparable from it; but if it refers to an accompanying circumstance, such as selling at the time of the call (to prayer), then it does not. What is in question here concerns an accompanying circumstance, namely the time of menstruation, so according to him it does not necessitate invalidity here either. This is supported by Ibn 'Umar being commanded to take her back, for if the divorce had not taken effect he would not have been commanded to do so. It has been said that his divorcing during menstruation was the occasion of the revelation of this verse, as narrated by Ibn Mardawayh through the route of Abu al-Zubayr from him, and it is also reported from al-Suddi.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muqatil, who said: "It has reached us that the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ (the verse) was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, Tufayl ibn al-Harith, and 'Amr ibn Sa'id ibn al-'As." Some said: some people did it, among them the son of 'Amr ibn al-'As and 'Utbah ibn Ghazwan, so the verse was revealed. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Sirin that it was revealed concerning Hafsah daughter of 'Umar, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) divorced once, so the verse was revealed down to His saying: ﴿He may bring about after that some matter﴾, and he (ﷺ) took her back. Qatadah narrated it from Anas. Al-Qurtubi said, quoting the scholars of hadith: the most sound view is that it was revealed initially to explain a legal ruling, and all the reasons for its revelation that have been mentioned do not stand as authentic. Abu Hayyan related something similar from the memorizer Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi. Its apparent meaning is that divorce itself is permissible, and this was also argued from what Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah narrated from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Among the most hateful of permitted things to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is divorce." In another wording: "The most hateful of lawful things to Allah is divorce." It is described as permitted and lawful; and since the elative form (af'al) is partly of what is attributed to it, and what is meant by its being hated is discouragement from it, or that it is hateful because it leads to severing the bond and loosing the tie of marriage, not because of its essence in itself.

Al-Bayhaqi said: the hatred is for pronouncing it at every time without regard to its prescribed time; and (there is the fact of) his (ﷺ) divorcing Hafsah and then Allah's command to him to take her back, for she is one who fasts much and stands much in prayer. Many others said: it is prohibited, because it involves ingratitude for the blessing of marriage, and because of his (ﷺ) saying: "Allah curses every man who tastes (women) much and divorces much." It is permitted only out of necessity. Ibn al-Humam said: this is the most sound view, so it is disliked when there is no necessity; and the word "permitted" is understood as referring to what is permitted at certain times, namely the times when the necessity that permits it is realized. This is evident in a narration of Abu Dawud: "Allah has not made lawful anything more hateful to Him than divorce," for an act has no generality across all times. Among the necessities is old age, and his lack of desire for intercourse with her to the point that he would be unable or would be harmed by forcing himself upon it, while she does not accept giving that up. As for what is reported from al-Hasan, who was asked about his frequent marrying and divorcing, and who said: "I love wealth" (or "I seek sufficiency") — Allah the Glorified said: ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾ [al-Nisa': 130] — this is his own opinion, if it is taken at face value. And all that is reported of the divorces of the Companions, such as the divorce of al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah of his four wives at once, in which he said to them: "You are of good character, of pleasing bodies, of long necks; go, for you are divorced," its meaning is to be understood as the existence of necessity, even if it was not stated.

Ibn Hajar said: it is either obligatory, as in the case of one who takes an oath to abstain (from his wife) and does not intend intercourse, and two arbitrators who judge so; or recommended, as when he is unable to fulfill her rights even through lack of inclination towards her; or when she is not chaste, provided he does not fear immorality by her. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) told one who said: "My wife does not turn away the hand of one who touches her," meaning she does not prevent anyone who intends immorality with her, according to one of the views on its meaning, by keeping her out of fear of that. Added to fear of immorality with her is the occurrence of hardship to him through separation from her that would lead to the permission of tayammum. Also the case where her staying with him is more protective against her immorality as far as appears, or where her character is bad, i.e., such that he will not customarily endure her company, as far as appears; otherwise, one whose character is not bad, like the rare white-crowed raven. Or one whose parent orders him to do it, i.e., without harshness, as is the habit of foolish fathers and mothers; and where there is no fear of trial or hardship from divorcing her, as far as appears; or it is forbidden, as in the innovative (bid'i) divorce; or it is disliked, where the situation is free of all of these, due to the sound hadith: "Nothing among the lawful is more hateful to Allah than divorce." And because it indicates greater discouragement from it, they said: there is nothing permitted in it. But al-Imam (al-Ghazali) interpreted it as the case where he has no appetite for her, meaning no complete desire, and his soul does not allow him to bear her expense without enjoyment. End quote.

As is not hidden from the fair-minded, the verse does not indicate more than its prohibition during menstruation. The women referred to in it are those who have been consummated with, who are observing the waiting period by menstruation, according to what is in the Kashshaf and others, because of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So divorce them for their waiting period﴾.

﴿And count the waiting period﴾: observe it and complete it as three full cycles (quru'). The original meaning of ihsa' is counting with pebbles, as was customary in earlier times, and then it became the established meaning for what has been mentioned. ﴿And fear Allah, your Lord﴾: regarding prolonging the waiting period for them and harming them. Describing Him with His lordship, Mighty and Majestic, addressed to them, is an emphasis on the command and an intensification in making taqwa obligatory. ﴿Do not turn them out of their houses﴾: from their dwellings at the time of divorce until their waiting period ends. Attributing the houses to them, though they belong to their husbands, serves to emphasize the prohibition by showing their full entitlement to residing in them, as if they were their own property. The absence of a conjunction indicates that the command stands independently, given attention. The prohibition of turning out includes, by its explicit wording, not turning them out in anger against them, or out of dislike for their company, or because of a need of theirs for the dwellings, or out of sheer foolishness. It also includes, by implication, not permitting them to go out, because their going out is forbidden by His saying: ﴿nor shall they go out﴾. As for when the particle is a prohibitive like the one before it, this is clear. As for when it is a negative, it is because what is meant is a prohibition, and that is more forceful than an explicit prohibition, as is not hidden. And permitting an act that is forbidden is itself forbidden, so it is as if it were said: do not turn them out, and do not permit them to go out when they request it, and they shall not go out on their own if they wish to. Thus there is an indication that their staying in the houses is a firmly established right of the Shari'ah, and so it is not cancelled by permission. This, as Al-Jalabi mentioned, is the position of the Hanafis. The position of the Shafi'is is that if the two of them agree on moving, it is permitted, since the right does not go beyond the two of them. So the meaning is: do not turn them out, and they shall not go out by their own independent decision. Al-Shihab criticized the attribution of this to the Hanafis, saying: "In it there is room for examination, and al-Razi mentioned in al-Ahkam what indicates the contrary, and that residence, like maintenance, is dropped by waiving it." End quote.

The most apparent reading of their statements is what al-Jalabi mentioned. Al-Haskafi also explicitly affirmed it in al-Durr al-Mukhtar (a key Hanafi legal text) and gave as its reason that this is a right of Allah the Exalted, so it does not lapse by the wife's permission. In al-Fath (Ibn al-Humam's commentary on al-Hidaya), it is stated that if a wife seeks khul' (divorce by compensation) on the condition that she has no residence right, then the husband's obligation to provide residence is nullified, and she is obliged to rent a dwelling. As for whether it becomes permissible for her to leave, it does not. ﴿except that they commit a flagrant immorality﴾, meaning, clearly evident, is itself leaving before the end of the waiting period (iddah), as related by Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, from Ibn Umar. It is also narrated from al-Suddi, Ibn al-Sa'ib and al-Nakha'i, and Abu Hanifa adopted this view. The exception here refers back to "they should not leave," and the meaning is: they are not permitted to leave except in a departure that is an immorality. It is known that they are not permitted to leave in that case either, so this amounts to a prohibition of leaving in the strongest form. Imam Ibn al-Humam said: "This is like what is said to the Khattabiyya: 'Do not commit adultery except if you are a fornicator, and do not insult your mother except if you are one who severs kinship,' and the like. It is extremely original and eloquent."

According to what is related from Qatada, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Dahhak, Ikrimah, Hammad and al-Layth, the immorality is adultery. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas, and Abu Yusuf adopted it. The exception here refers back to "do not expel them," as the apparent meaning of the statements of a group implies, that is: do not expel them except if they commit adultery, in which case expel them in order to carry out the prescribed punishment upon them. Some researchers said: it refers to all of them, and to whatever requires a prescribed punishment, whether adultery, theft or other, as related by Abd ibn Humayd from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, and al-Tabari chose this view. The immorality is abusive speech against the in-laws, or against the husband, as related by a group through several chains from Ibn Abbas. The exception refers to the first, meaning: do not expel them except when their tongues grow long and they speak foul and ugly speech to their husbands or their in-laws. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy, "﴿unless they commit indecency against you﴾," with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the ha'. In Muwashshah al-Ahwazi it is "yufhishna," from afhasha. Al-Jawhari said: afhasha 'alayhi fi al-nutq, meaning he uttered obscenity. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, "illa an yafhishna," without "alaykum." And the disobedience (nushuz) is intended, meaning: except that they be divorced for disobedience, as related from Qatada as well. The exception regarding this is said to refer to the first also. In al-Kashf it is said that it refers to all of them, because when her right to residence lapses, expulsion and leaving become permissible too. Whichever of these is the case, the verse does not restrict what permits doing the forbidden thing to committing an immorality. The permissible matters have been set out in the books of the furu' (branches of jurisprudence), so whoever wishes should consult them.

Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr read "mubayyinah" with a fatha. ﴿These are﴾ refers to the rulings mentioned, meaning: these great rulings. ﴿the limits of Allah﴾ which He appointed for His servants, Mighty and Majestic is He. ﴿And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah﴾, meaning His limits, Exalted is He, mentioned above, by neglecting any part of them. The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is to magnify the matter of transgression and to indicate the reason for the ruling in His saying: ﴿has certainly wronged himself﴾, meaning he has harmed himself, as Shaykh al-Islam said. He related from some (commentators) that wronging (zulm) is interpreted as exposing oneself to punishment. He criticized this, saying that the statement of the Exalted, ﴿You do not know; perhaps Allah will bring about after that some matter﴾, contradicts it, since it is a resumed statement given to explain the content of the conditional clause. They have said that the matter Allah brings about is that He turns the heart of the transgressor away from what he did by transgression to its opposite. Therefore the wronging must be a worldly harm that befalls him because of his transgression and that he cannot remedy, or it refers to harm in general, encompassing both worldly and otherworldly harm. The explanation was restricted to the worldly harm because most people's guard against it is stronger and their concern to avert it is greater.

It was rebutted by saying that worldly harm is not certain, so wronging should not be interpreted here as that. Also, the statement of the Exalted, ﴿You do not know﴾ and so on, is not an explanation of what was mentioned; rather, it is an encouragement to observe the limits after the warning. In this there is that it resembles a warning more than an encouragement. Perhaps the intended meaning of "harmed himself" is that he exposed himself to harm, so the wronging is that exposure, and there is no objection to interpreting it that way, as far as appears. The clause of hope is in the accusative position governed by ﴿You do not know﴾. Abu Hayyan counted "la'alla" among the suspensive particles. The address in ﴿You do not know﴾ is to the transgressor by way of iltifat (shift of address), to add emphasis to the warning against transgression, not to the Prophet (ﷺ), as has been said. So the meaning is: whoever transgresses the limits of Allah the Exalted has exposed himself to harm, for you do not know, O transgressor, the outcome of the matter, ﴿perhaps Allah﴾ the Exalted will bring about in your heart ﴿after that﴾ which you did of transgression ﴿some matter﴾ that requires the opposite of what you did, so that hatred of her becomes love, and turning away from her becomes turning toward her. It cannot be remedied by a return (raj'ah) or by a new marriage contract (isti'naf)

**Page 135**

﴿When they have reached their term﴾ means they were about to complete their waiting period (ʿiddah).

﴿Then retain them﴾ means take them back (rajʿah), ﴿in kindness﴾ meaning with good companionship and maintenance suited to the circumstances, from both sides.

﴿Or part from them in kindness﴾ means by paying what is due and avoiding harm, such as when a man takes her back and then divorces her again in order to prolong the waiting period.

﴿And call to witness two just men from among you﴾ refers to the time of the return (rajʿah), if you choose it, or of separation, if you choose it, to remove suspicion and to end disputes. This is a command of recommendation (nadb, a recommended act, not an obligation), as in His words, ﴿and call witnesses when you conclude a sale﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 282). Al-Shafiʿi, in his older view (al-qawl al-qadim), held that it is obligatory for the return. Al-Tabarsi claimed that the apparent meaning is that he commanded calling witnesses for the divorce, that this is related from the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt, may God be pleased with them all, that it is obligatory, and that it is a condition for the validity of the divorce.

﴿And establish the testimony﴾ means, O witnesses, when it is needed, ﴿for God﴾, sincerely for His sake, may He be exalted. The verse also provides evidence against the view of those who say that when two commands are joined by a conjunction and addressed to two different persons, the vocative (ندا, nida, calling out) must be mentioned, or its omission is considered ugly, as in اضْرِبْ يا زَيْدُ وقُمْ يا عَمْرُو ("Strike, O Zayd, and stand up, O ʿAmr"). And as for those who restrict the permissibility of omitting it without ugliness to cases where the two commands differ, as in His words, ﴿Joseph, turn away from this, and ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ (Yusuf: 29), then the one commanded by His words ﴿call to witness﴾ is the divorcing men, and the one commanded by His words, glorified is He, ﴿establish the testimony﴾ is the witnesses, as we have pointed out. It has been joined by conjunction without difference in the most eloquent speech.

﴿This is admonished to whoever believes in God and the Last Day﴾ means because he is the one who benefits from it. The reference, according to what the author of al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari) chose, is to the exhortation to establish testimony for God, may He be exalted. The better view, as in al-Kashf (al-Tibi), is that it refers to everything mentioned before: pronouncing the divorce in accordance with the Sunnah, counting the waiting period, not expelling them from their homes nor their leaving, and establishing testimony for the return or the separation, so that it fits more closely with His words, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And whoever fears God, He will make for him a way out﴾.

"And He will provide for him from where he does not expect." This is an interjection (i'tiraḍ) placed between two coordinated clauses, brought to affirm the rulings mentioned earlier with the promise attached to fearing Allah regarding them. The meaning is: whoever fears Allah, the Exalted, by divorcing in accordance with the Sunnah, not harming the woman in her waiting period (ʿiddah), not expelling her from her dwelling, and taking precaution by calling witnesses, Allah, Glorified is He, will make for him a way out of whatever distress may arise in matters of spouses, of sorrows and of falling into straits, and will relieve him of the anxieties that befall him, and will provide for him from a direction that does not occur to his mind and that he does not reckon.

Reports from some of the Companions — such as ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, and Ibn ʿAbbās in some narrations from him — contain, on their apparent sense, what supports this reading. It is also permitted that it be an interjection placed by way of digression (istiṭrād) when mentioning the words of the Exalted: "That is what you are admonished with" etc. The meaning then is: whoever fears Allah, the Exalted, in all that he does and leaves undone, He will make for him a way out from the distresses of this world and the Hereafter. This is preferable because of the generality of the benefit, its inclusion of what we are dealing with as a primary inclusion, and because reports concerning the occasion of revelation and others require it.

Abū Yaʿlā, Abū Nuʿaym and al-Daylamī narrated through the chain of ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited His words, the Exalted: 'And whoever fears Allah' etc., and said: 'A way out from the doubts of this world, from the agonies of death, and from the hardships of the Day of Resurrection.'"

Aḥmad, al-Ḥākim — who graded it sound — Ibn Mardawayh, Abū Nuʿaym in al-Maʿrifah, and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Abū Dharr, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began reciting this verse: 'And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out' and 'And will provide for him from where he does not expect,' and he kept repeating it until I became drowsy. Then he said: 'O Abū Dharr, if all the people were to hold fast to it, it would suffice them.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated through al-Kalbī, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "ʿAwf ibn Mālik al-Ashjaʿī came and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, my son has been captured by the enemy, and his mother is distressed. What do you command me?' He said: 'I command you and her to repeat often: there is no power and no strength except in Allah.' The woman said: 'What an excellent command he has given you!' So they both repeated it often, and the enemy became careless, and he drove off their sheep and brought them to his father. Then the verse was revealed: 'And whoever fears Allah.'" etc.

In the narration of Ibn Abī Ḥātim from Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, client of the family of Qays, who said: "ʿAwf ibn Mālik al-Ashjaʿī came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said to him: 'Ibn ʿAwf has been captured.' He said to him, peace and blessings be upon him: 'Send to him that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commands you to repeat often: there is no power and no strength except in Allah.' They had bound him with rawhide, and the rawhide fell from him, so he went out and found a camel of theirs, mounted it, and found a herd of the people who had bound him. He shouted at them, and the last of them followed the first, and he did not surprise his parents except that he was calling at the door. His father came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him, and the verse was revealed: 'And whoever fears Allah'" etc.

In some narrations, he suffered hardship and affliction and complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Fear Allah and be patient." Then his son returned, having seized some goats. He mentioned that to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and the verse was revealed. He said: "It is yours." And other narrations of this kind are confused, as is not hidden from one who investigates them. According to the view of digression, it has been said: the meaning is, whoever avoids the unlawful, He will make for him a way out to the lawful. It has been said: a way out from hardship to ease; it has been said: from the Fire to Paradise; and it has been said: a way out from punishment, "and He will provide for him from where he does not expect" — from reward. Al-Kalbī said: "Whoever fears Allah" at the time of calamity, "He will make for him a way out" to Paradise. All of these, as you see, [are weak], and what is relied upon is the generality you have heard. In al-Kashshāf: the diversification of the promise to the God-fearing and the repetition of exhortation to it, after the indication that taqwā is the basis of the matter with Allah, to which He attached the happiness of both abodes, indicates that the matter of divorce and ʿiddah is among the matters that need abundant taqwā, because it is the most detestable of permissible things to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for what it entails of alienation and severing of the familiarity that paves the way. Then, precaution regarding lineage, which is among the greatest objectives, indicates strictness in the matter of ʿiddah. Taqwā is therefore necessary so that divorce occurs in a manner for which one is praised, and so that what is obligatory in ʿiddah is observed with precaution; thereby the spouses attain a way out in this world and the Hereafter. Accordingly, the wife is included in the generality just as the husband is. "And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him," that is, sufficient for him, the Mighty and Majestic, in all his affairs.

Aḥmad narrated in al-Zuhd from Wahb, who said: "The Lord, blessed and exalted, says: When My servant relies upon Me, even if the heavens and the earth were to plot against him, I would make for him a way out from among them." "Indeed, Allah accomplishes His command" — with the attributive participle idāfah to its object; the original would be bāligh amrahu with the accusative, as most readers recited it — that is, He attains what He wills, the Mighty and Majestic, and no desired thing escapes Him.

Ibn Abī ʿAbla in one narration, Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind, and ʿIṣmah from Abū ʿAmr read "bāligh" with nominative and tanwīn, "amruhu" with nominative as the agent of "bāligh" — the predicate — since "inna"... or as subject, with "bāligh" as predicate preceding it, and the clause is the predicate of "inna," meaning: His command is carried out, the Mighty and Majestic. Al-Mufaḍḍal in one narration also read "bāligan" with accusative and "amruhu" with nominative. This is explained as "bāligan" being a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the agent of "jaʿala" in His words, the Exalted: "Allah has indeed set a measure for everything," not from the subject, because they do not approve of a ḥāl coming from it; and the clause "qad jaʿala" etc. is the predicate of "inna." It is also permitted that "bāligan" be the predicate itself according to the dialect of those who put both parts in the accusative after "inna," as in the verse:

"When the darkness of night turns black, come, and let your steps be light, for our guards are lions."

It has been criticized that this is a weak dialect. The meaning of "qadran" is "measure," and what is intended is its determination before its existence, or a measure of time. This is an explanation of the obligation of relying upon Allah, the Exalted, and committing the matter to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, for when it is known that everything, of provision and otherwise, occurs only by His determination, the Exalted, nothing remains but submission to the decree. It contains, as has been said, a confirmation of what preceded regarding the timing of divorce and the command to count the ʿiddah, and a preparation for what will come, God willing, concerning its durations.

Jannāḥ ibn Ḥubaysh read "qadaran" with a fatḥah on the dāl.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 65, verse 4:

﴿And those of your women who have despaired of menstruation﴾, i.e., of menstruation (al-hayd). It is also read as "yayisna" (in the present tense), ﴿from among your women﴾ due to their old age. Some have estimated the age of despair (sin al-ya's) as sixty years, and others as fifty-five. It was said: it is the typical age of despair among the woman's kin (al-'ashira). It was also said: it is the typical age of despair among women in the place where they live, for if a place has good air and water, such as some deserts, the age of despair is delayed there. It was also said: it is the furthest custom of any woman in the world, and this saying, reaching the degree of despair, is too far to be accepted. ﴿If you are in doubt﴾, i.e., if you are uncertain and hesitant regarding their waiting period, or if you do not know their waiting period, ﴿then their waiting period is three months﴾. Al-Hakim narrated it and declared it sound, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, and a group from Ubayy ibn Ka'b

Page 137

that when some people of Madinah heard the verse in al-Baqarah about the waiting period of women, they said: "There remain among the waiting periods of women some categories not mentioned in the Qur'an: the young and the old, those whose menstruation has ceased, and pregnant women." So God the Exalted revealed in Surat al-Nisa' al-Qusra (the shorter Surat al-Nisa'): ﴿And those who have despaired﴾, the verse. In another narration, a group among them, including Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Khallad ibn al-Nu'man, when they heard His saying the Exalted: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228], said: "O Messenger of God, what is the waiting period of one who has no period due to youth or old age?" Then ﴿And those who have despaired﴾ etc. was revealed. Someone said: "What is the waiting period of a pregnant woman?" Then ﴿And those with children (ulat al-ahmal)﴾ etc. was revealed.

It is known from what has been mentioned that the condition here has no implicit meaning (mafhum) according to those who hold the doctrine of mafhum, because it is an explanation of the event in which it was revealed, without intent to restrict. The assumed object of the doubt, "what you have heard," is what al-Tabari and others indicated. It was also said: ﴿If you are in doubt﴾ concerning the blood of women who have reached the limit of despair, whether it is blood of menstruation or of istihada (irregular bleeding), then their waiting period is etc. If this is the waiting period of a woman about whom there is doubt, then a woman about whom there is no doubt is more deserving of it. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is ﴿If you are in doubt﴾ regarding their menstruation, when the blood has ceased from them and they are of the kind who menstruate like them. Mujahid said: the verse concerns the mustahadah (the woman with continuous bleeding) whom the blood has overwhelmed, not knowing whether it is menstrual blood or blood of illness. It was also said: ﴿If you are in doubt﴾ means: if you are certain of their despair. Doubt (al-irtiyab) is among the words with opposite meanings (al-adhdad), and all of these, as you see, are far-fetched.

The relative pronoun (al-mawsul): they said it is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is the clause ﴿then their waiting period﴾ etc. "If you are in doubt" is a conditional clause whose response is omitted, its estimate being "then know that it is three months." The conditional clause and its response are interposed clauses. It is also permitted that ﴿then their waiting period﴾ etc. be the response of the condition, in terms of informing and reporting, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from God﴾ [al-Nahl: 53]; the conditional sentence is a predicate without omission or estimation. His saying the Exalted: ﴿And those who have not menstruated﴾ is a subject whose predicate is omitted, i.e., "and those who have not menstruated, likewise," or "their waiting period is three months," and the clause is conjoined to what precedes it. It is also permitted to conjoin this relative pronoun to the preceding relative pronoun and to make one predicate for both without estimation. What is meant by "those who have not menstruated" is the young ones who have not reached the age of menstruation.

Abu Hayyan preferred that it includes those who have not menstruated due to youth, those who will never have menstruation at all, like some women who live until they die without menstruating, and those whose time of menstruation has passed without their having menstruated. Then he said: It was said: this one observes a waiting period of one year.

﴿And for those with children (ulat al-ahmal), their term (ajaluhunna)﴾, i.e., the end of their waiting period, ﴿is that they deliver their burden (hamlahunna)﴾, even if it is a small lump of flesh or a clot. There is no difference in this between those who are divorced and those whose husbands have died, as was narrated from Umar and his son. Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Umar that he was asked about a woman whose husband died while she was pregnant, and he said: "When she delivers her burden, she is free." A man of the Ansar informed him that Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "Even if she gave birth while her husband was on his bier before he was buried, she would be free." From Ibn Mas'ud: Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated from him that he said: "Whoever wishes, I will invoke a curse upon him (la'anatuhu), that the verse in Surat al-Nisa' al-Qusra, ﴿And those with children﴾ etc., was revealed after Surat al-Baqarah by so-and-so many months, and every divorced woman or widow, her term is that she deliver her burden." In a narration of Ibn Mardawayh from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "after seven years," but this perhaps is not sound. From Abu Hurayrah, Abu Mas'ud al-Badri and A'ishah, and to this the jurists of the cities (fuqaha' al-amsar) went, and it was narrated from the Messenger of God ﷺ. Abd ibn Humayd in the Zawa'id of al-Musnad, Abu Ya'la, al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated: "From Ubayy ibn Ka'b who said: I said to the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿And those with children, their term is that they deliver their burden﴾ — is it for the divorced thrice and the widowed?" He said: "It is for the divorced thrice and the widowed." A group narrated something similar from him by another route. And it is authentically narrated that Subay'ah bint al-Harith al-Aslamiyyah was married to Sa'd ibn Khawlah, and he died leaving her in the Farewell Pilgrimage while she was pregnant, and she delivered twenty-three days after his death; in another narration, twenty-five nights; in another, forty nights. She dyed her hands, applied kohl and adorned herself, wishing to remarry, and this was disapproved of her. The Prophet ﷺ was asked, and he said: "If you do so, her term has ended." Ali, may God ennoble his face, and Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, held that the verse concerns divorced women, while for a widow her waiting period is the later of the two terms, and this is the doctrine of the Imamiyyah as in Majma' al-Bayan.

According to what has preceded, the verse abrogates the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And those of you who die and leave wives shall wait by themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 234], the verse, according to the view of the followers of Abu Hanifah and those who agree with them among the Shafi'is, because a general, absolute, later text abrogates in their view; so it is more fitting that a general-from-one-aspect text should be so. As for one who does not hold this, one who does not permit delaying the explanation of a general text says: by abrogation as well, because the first general text at that time has its scope over its individuals, and in such a case there is no disagreement that a later specific text abrogates to its extent, not merely specifies. Whoever permits it holds to specification, on the basis that the one in al-Qusra is more specific absolutely. Its reasoning is that in al-Baqarah the ruling for divorced women and the ruling for widowed women were stated separately; then this verse came specifying both sections, since the word "ajal" covers both waiting periods, and "ulat al-ahmal" is specific absolutely with respect to wives. This is like one saying: "The Hindi clients have such-and-such, and their Turkish ones have such-and-such for another category; then he says: and their elders have less than that, or more, or such-and-such," meaning another class; the latter specifies both rulings, and no attention is paid to the difference in gifts, because the word covering exclusivity and the specificity of elders among clients is absolute in the same way. In our matter, no attention is paid to the difference of the two waiting periods, because of the word "ajal" covering and the specificity of "ulat al-ahmal" absolutely with respect to husbands. If you wish, say: with respect to divorced women and widows whose husbands are absolutely their men; so there is no difference, as stated in al-Kashf. Then he said: Whoever holds the longer of the two terms argues that the two texts reinforce each other, since between them there is general and specific in one respect, and there is no ground for nullifying either, so combination is required. In this view combination is achieved, because if the period of pregnancy is longer, she has waited four months and ten days along with the excess; and if it is shorter, she has waited the period and delivered, and waited; so action is achieved according to the two verses. The answer is that this is nullification of the two texts, not combination, since what is considered is combining the two texts, not the two periods, and that is because the limitation and timing, which is the requirement of the two verses, is lost. End quote. So reflect.

Abu al-Dahhak read "ahmalahunna" in the plural. ﴿And whoever fears God﴾ regarding His rulings and observing their rights: ﴿He will make for him of his affair ease﴾, by God, Mighty and Majestic, making his affair easy for him. It was said: ease is reward. "Min" (whoever) is said to be explanatory, placed before what it explains for the sake of the rhyme; it was said: it means "in"; it was said:

ذَلِكَ ("That") refers to the rulings mentioned above, and the demonstrative carries the sense of distance to signal the elevated rank of these rulings in excellence. The kaf (the "-ka" of dhalika) is in the singular, even though the address is plural, as is made clear by God's words: ﴿The command of God, which He has sent down to you﴾. The reason is that the kaf here serves merely to distinguish between what is present and what has passed, and not to specify the particular identity of those addressed. ﴿And whoever fears God﴾ by guarding His rulings, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿He will remove from him his misdeeds﴾, for good deeds remove misdeeds. ﴿And He will magnify for him his reward﴾ by multiplying it. Al-A'mash read nu'azzimu ("We will magnify") with the nun, an iltifat (shift) from the third person to the first person of speech. Ibn Muqsim read yu'azzimu ("He will magnify") with the ya' and with shadda, the present tense of 'azzama in its intensive form.

[p. 139]

God's words, ﴿House them where you dwell﴾, form a resumed sentence (isti'naf, a new sentence that answers an implied question). It answers a question arising from what precedes it, the exhortation to taqwa (God-consciousness). It is as if it were said: "How do we act upon taqwa concerning the women in waiting (mu'taddat)?" So it is said: ﴿House them﴾, etc. The min here is partitive (lil-tab'id), meaning: house them in part of your dwelling-place, and let them reside in some corner of it if there is only one house, as narrated from Qatada. Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' said that it is for the beginning of the end-point (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). God's words, ﴿according to your means﴾, mean: according to your capacity, that is, what you are able to bear. It is an explicatory apposition ('atf bayan) to God's words ﴿where you dwell﴾, according to what al-Zamakhshari said. Abu Hayyan refuted this, saying that no explicatory apposition is known in which the governing element is repeated; this is rather the manner of a substitute (badal) with a preposition. For this reason Abu al-Baqa' parsed it as a substitute. It was objected that the intended meaning is that the prepositional phrase is an explicatory apposition to the prepositional phrase, not merely to the genitive noun, so that this objection would apply; yet this is not cogent for him, and there is no difference between explicatory apposition and substitute except in a minor matter. The force of Abu Hayyan's statement is not hidden. Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Ibn Abi 'Abla and Abu Haywa read ﴿min wujdikum﴾ with a fatha on the waw; al-Fayyad ibn Ghazwan, 'Amr ibn Maymun and Ya'qub read it with a kasra, and al-Mahdawi mentioned it from al-A'raj. The meaning in all readings is the capacity (al-wus').

﴿And do not harm them﴾: do not employ harm toward them in the matter of housing; ﴿in order to constrict them﴾: so that you compel them to leave by occupying the space, or by housing with them someone whom they do not wish to live with, and the like.

﴿And if they are﴾, that is, the divorced women, ﴿pregnant, then spend upon them until they deliver their burden﴾, so that they exit the waiting period (iddah). As for widows, there is no maintenance (nafaqah) for them according to most scholars. From 'Ali, may God honor his face, and Ibn Mas'ud, it is narrated that their maintenance is obligatory from the estate. There is no disagreement on the obligation of housing and maintenance for pregnant divorced women, whether the divorce was irrevocable (batt) or not.

There is disagreement concerning non-pregnant divorced women, after agreement that housing is due to them when they are not irrevocably divorced. Ibn al-Musayyab, Sulayman ibn Yasar, 'Ata', al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan, Malik, al-Awza'i, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Shafi'i and Abu 'Ubayd said: a non-pregnant irrevocably divorced woman has housing, and has no maintenance. Al-Hasan, Hammad, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr and the Imamiyya said: she has neither housing nor maintenance, based on the hadith of Fatima bint Qays, who said: "My husband Abu 'Amr ibn Hafs ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi divorced me irrevocably (al-batta), so I brought my case to the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, regarding housing and maintenance, and he did not grant me housing or maintenance, and he ordered me to observe the waiting period in the house of Ibn Umm Maktum; then he married me to Usama ibn Zayd." Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri said: she has housing and maintenance. Their proof is that "'Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: I heard the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, say concerning the irrevocably divorced woman: 'She has maintenance and housing.'" Together with this, that is the recompense of confinement (al-ihtibas), which is shared between the non-pregnant and the pregnant. If it were a recompense for the pregnancy, it would be due from her husband's property if he had property, and they did not say this.

This is confirmed by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "House them where you dwell, and spend upon them according to your means." As for one who restricted spending to pregnant women in the waiting period, he derived evidence from this verse because of the condition in it. This does not hold for those who deny the implicit contrary meaning (mafhum al-mukhalafa). Moreover, the benefit of the condition here is that a pregnant woman might be supposed to have no maintenance because of the long duration of pregnancy, so He established maintenance for her, so that others might be known by the more fitting inference (bi-al-tariq al-awla), as in the Kashshaf. Thus it is from the implicit agreeing meaning (mafhum al-muwafaqa). The hadith of Fatima bint Qays has been criticized by 'Umar, 'A'isha, Sulayman ibn Yasar, al-Aswad ibn Yazid, Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Rahman and others.

﴿And if they nurse for you﴾, that is, after they have delivered their burden, ﴿then give them their wages﴾ for the suckling. ﴿And confer among yourselves in kindness﴾: this is addressed to the fathers and mothers. The form iftaʿala (ift'ala) is in the sense of tafa'ala (mutual action). It is said: "the people conferred (ita'mara) and they consulted each other (ta'amaru), with the same meaning." Al-Kisa'i said: the meaning is "they consulted." Its real sense is that each should command the other with what is kind, regarding the wage and the suckling; there should be neither niggardliness (mumasakah) on the father's part nor hardship (mu'asarah) on the mother's part. It was also said: "kindness" means clothing and covering.

﴿And if you disagree﴾, that is, you are constrained, meaning one of you constrains the other by haggling over the wage, or by demanding an increase, or the like. ﴿Then another woman will nurse for him﴾: that is, another wet-nurse will be found, and no nurse will be lacking. It is said that in this there is a rebuke to the mother, since it is like your saying to someone from whom you request a need and who then makes excuses: "Someone else will fulfill it," meaning: "It will be fulfilled, while you are blameworthy."

Ibn al-Munir said that the mother is singled out for rebuke because what is given on her part is her milk for her child, which is not regarded as property and is not customarily guaranteed, especially from a mother to her child. This is not so with what is given on the father's part, which is property, customarily withheld. Thus the mother is more deserving of blame and more entitled to reproach. The sense is: "Let the father seek another nurse for him," and then the connection between condition and consequence becomes evident. Some eminent scholars said: the speech is not free of rebuke of the father as well, since in the apodosis the address has been dropped from the dignity of direct address, with an indication that if he constrains the mother over the wage and she refuses to nurse for that reason, then another woman must nurse; she too usually seeks a wage, while the mother is more compassionate and thus more fitting for it. With this the full connection appears. The first view is more evident, so reflect.

It was also said: ﴿then will nurse﴾ is a report with the meaning of a command: "let her nurse." But this is not the case. This ruling applies when the infant accepts another breast. As for when it accepts only its mother's breast, they have said: she is compelled to nurse for the wage of her equivalent.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 65, verse 7:

﴿Let the one of wealth spend from his wealth, and whoever has his provision restricted, let him spend from what Allah has given him﴾, meaning, *ḍuyyiqa* (was restricted) ﴿for him, his provision﴾, even if it is little. The intended meaning is that each one, the wealthy and the poor alike, should spend what his capacity reaches. The apparent reading is that the ones commanded to spend are the fathers. From here Ibn al-'Arabi said: this verse is the basis for the obligation of maintenance (nafaqa, the financial support owed to dependants) upon the father. Muhammad ibn al-Mawwaz disagreed on this, saying that it is obligatory upon both parents according to their share of inheritance. Abu Mu'adh reported that it was read *li-yunfiqa* with the *lam* of purpose and a *fatḥa* on the *qāf*, on the basis that the implied meaning is: "We have legislated that so that he may spend." Ibn Abi 'Abla read *qudira* with the *dāl* shaddah (doubled), ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond what He has given it﴾, meaning, beyond what capacity He has given it. It was also said: what He has given it of provisions, be it little or much. In this there is consolation and winning over the heart of the poor, because of the specific use of the word *ātāhā* (He has given it) here, which was previously tied to restriction, and the mention of hardship after it. Those who hold that there is no annulment of marriage due to inability to maintain the wife have used this verse as evidence. This is the view adopted by 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Abu Hanifa and a group of scholars. Yet it is reported from Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan, Ibn al-Musayyab, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq that the marriage is annulled due to inability to maintain, and the spouses are separated. The verse also contains, as al-Suyuti said, the recommendation that a person take into account his own condition in maintenance and charity. Thus in the hadith: "Indeed the believer has taken from Allah, the Exalted, a good manner: when He, glory be to Him, grants him abundance, he grants abundance (in turn), and when He, Mighty and Majestic, restricts provision for him, he restricts."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah will bring about, after hardship, ease﴾ is a promise to the poor of that time that the doors of provision will be opened for them, or to the poor spouses if they spend what they are able to and do not fall short. It is, on both interpretations, a *tadhyīl* (a concluding statement appended to a sentence that generalises its meaning). However, on the first interpretation it is independent (*mustaqill*), and on the second it is not independent.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 65, verse 8:

﴿And how many a city﴾ means: many of the people of a city.

Ibn Kathir recited «wa-ka'in» (وكائِنٌ) with a long vowel and a hamza, and the detailed discussion of it has already passed. ﴿Rebelled (ʿatat)﴾ means: became arrogant and haughty, turning away ﴿from the command of its Lord and His messengers﴾, so it did not comply with that. ﴿So We called it to account with a severe reckoning﴾, with thorough scrutiny, probing, and close examination, ﴿for every speck of sin and every trifle﴾.

﴿And We punished it with a dreadful punishment (ʿadhaban nukran)﴾, meaning a great, abhorrent punishment. What is intended is the reckoning and punishment of the Hereafter, and the expression of both in the past tense serves to indicate their certainty, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown﴾ [al-Kahf: 99], and others.

Some readers recited «nukur» (نُكُرًا) with two dammas.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 65, verse 9:

﴿So she tasted the evil consequence of her affair﴾ — the punishment for her defiance (ʿutuww); ﴿and the outcome of her affair was a loss﴾ — a terrible loss, beyond which there is no further loss.

Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment. This is a repetition of the threat and an explanation of what necessitates the taqwa (God-consciousness) commanded by His saying, ﴿so fear Allah, O people of understanding﴾. It is as if it were said: Allah the Exalted has prepared this punishment for them, so let this be a motive for you, O people of understanding, to fear Allah the Exalted and to beware of His punishment. Al-Kalbi said: the speech is in the form of inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir, "fronting and postponing"), and what is meant is: "We punished it with a terrible punishment" in this world, through hunger, famine, the sword, and all other calamities and trials, ﴿and We called it to a severe account﴾ in the Hereafter.

The apparent meaning is that His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Allah has prepared﴾ and so on, is also a repetition of the threat. It is also permissible that the severe reckoning means the thorough recording of their sins and their inscription in the scrolls of the recording angels (al-hafaza), and that the terrible punishment means what befell them swiftly. The clause ﴿they defied﴾ and so on may be taken as a description of "a town," and the past tense in ﴿and We called it to account﴾ is then used. The word "ʿadhdhabnāhā" is taken literally. The predicate of "kaʾayyin" (how many) is the clause ﴿Allah has prepared﴾ and so on; or the clause ﴿they defied﴾ and so on is itself the predicate, and the clause ﴿Allah has prepared﴾ and so on is a resumed (istiʾnaf) sentence explaining that their punishment is not confined to what has been mentioned, but that there is a severe punishment for them after it.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿those who believe﴾ is in the accusative by an implied "aʿnī" (I mean), as an explanation of the preceding vocative; or it is an adjective (naʿt) of it; or it is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to it. Making it a substitute (badal) from it is weak, because it cannot properly occupy its position.

﴿Allah has certainly sent down to you a reminder﴾: the "reminder" is the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. It is expressed by this term about him because of his constancy in reciting the Qur'an, which is a reminder, or in conveying it and admonishing by it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 65, verse 11:**

Allah's words ﴿a Messenger﴾ are an apposition (*badal*, a substitute or appositive) for what precedes it. He expressed His sending (*irsal*) by the word "sending down" (*inzal*) as a *tarshih* (a device that reinforces the metaphor, here *tarshih* meaning the reinforcement of a figurative usage) for the figurative sense. Alternatively, sending is a consequence of sending down, so ﴿sent down﴾ is a *majaz mursal* (metonymy, a figurative usage based on a non-metaphorical relation between the literal and intended meanings).

Abu Hayyan said: "The apparent meaning is that the Reminder (*dhikr*) is the Qur'an and the Messenger is Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Then either the Reminder itself is made a figurative usage, or it is an apposition with an omitted modifier (*hadhf mudaf*), meaning: one possessing a reminder, a Messenger. In that case ﴿a Messenger﴾ is a qualifier (*na't*, an adjective) of that omitted noun, or an apposition." It was also said that ﴿a Messenger﴾ is in the accusative governed by an implied verb, such as "He sent a Messenger," which is indicated by "sent down." This is the view of as-Suddi, and Ibn Atiyya chose it. Al-Zajjaj and Abu Ali said that it may be an object (*ma'mul*) of the verbal noun *dhikr*, as in His words: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger, an orphan﴾ [al-Balad: 14–15], and in the words of the poet:

*With strikes of swords on the heads of a people, we removed their skulls from their resting places.*

That is: ﴿Allah sent down﴾ His Reminder ﴿a Messenger﴾, in the sense that Allah, mighty and majestic, sent down what indicates His honour with Him and His nearness (*zulfa*). It is said that by this is meant the Qur'an, but this involves forced interpretation (*ta'assuf*). Similarly, ﴿a Messenger﴾ may be taken as an apposition of it, on the basis that it means the message (*risala*).

Al-Kalbi said: "The Messenger here is Jibril, peace be upon him." He also made it an apposition of ﴿Reminder﴾. The application of the term "Reminder" to him is because of his frequent remembrance (of Allah), so it is a description by a verbal noun for emphasis, like "a just man" (*rajul adl*). Or it is because he descends with the Reminder, which is the Qur'an, so there is a connection between them like that of inherence (*hulul*). Or it is because he, peace be upon him, is mentioned in the heavens and among the nations, so the verbal noun has the sense of a passive participle, as in "a dirham of the amir's minting" (*dirham darb al-amir*). In that case, "Reminder" may be explained as "honour," as in His words: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44]. Thus it is as if he were in himself an honour, either because he is an honour to the one upon whom he was sent down, or because he possesses glory and honour with Allah, mighty and majestic, as in His words: ﴿with the Possessor of the Throne, firmly established﴾ [al-Takwir: 20].

[Page 142]

In al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari's commentary): if by "Reminder" the Qur'an is meant, and by "Messenger" Jibril, peace be upon him, then the apposition is a *badal al-ishtimal* (an apposition of inclusion, where the second term is a part or aspect of the first in a looser relation). If by "Reminder" honour or something else is meant, then it is a *badal al-kull* (an apposition of the whole, where the second term is identical in extent to the first). So consider this carefully.

It is also read as ﴿Messenger﴾ (*rasul*, in the nominative), with an implied pronoun *huwa* (he). His words ﴿reciting to you the signs of Allah, clarifying﴾ are a qualifier of ﴿Messenger﴾ (in the accusative), and this is the apparent reading. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of the name "Allah," exalted is He; attributing recitation to Him is figurative, like "the amir built the city." ﴿The signs of Allah﴾ means the Qur'an. In this there is the placing of an apparent noun in the place of a pronoun, according to one of the views. The word *mubayyinat* (clarifying) is a circumstantial clause of them, meaning: in a state of making clear to you what you need of rulings. It is also read *mubayyanat* (made clear), meaning that Allah has made them clear, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿We have already made the signs clear for you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 118; al-Hadid: 17].

The *lam* in His words ﴿that He may bring out those who believe and do righteous deeds from darknesses into light﴾ is connected either to ﴿sent down﴾ or to ﴿reciting﴾. The subject of ﴿brings out﴾ according to the second view is the pronoun referring to the Messenger, upon whom be blessings and peace, or the pronoun referring to Him, mighty and majestic. The relative clause refers either to the believers after the sending down of the Reminder and before the revelation of this verse, or to those whom Allah, exalted is He, knew and decreed would believe. That is: so that the Messenger, or Allah, mighty and majestic, may bring about for them what they are now upon of faith and righteous deeds; or so that He may bring out from various kinds of misguidance to guidance those whom He knew and decreed would believe. The past tense is either with regard to the revelation of this verse, or with regard to His knowledge and His eternal decree, exalted is He.

﴿And whoever believes in Allah and does righteous deeds﴾, as is made clear in the midst of what has been sent down of the clarifying signs.

﴿He will admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. Nafi' and Ibn Amir read *nudkhilhu* with the first person plural of majesty (*nun al-azama*). His words ﴿abiding therein forever﴾ are a circumstantial clause of the object of ﴿He will admit him﴾. The plural is in view of the sense of *man* (whoever), just as the singular in the three pronouns is in view of its wording. His words ﴿Allah has granted him a good provision﴾ are another circumstantial clause of him, or of the pronoun in "abiding," by way of *tadakhul* (interpenetration of two circumstantial clauses). The singular of the pronoun "him" is also in view of the wording. There is in it the sense of wonder and magnification of what Allah, exalted is He, has granted the believers of reward. Otherwise, the report of what is mentioned here would have little benefit, as is not hidden.

Most grammarians have used this verse as evidence for the permissibility of observing the wording first, then observing the sense, then observing the wording again (*mura'at al-lafz thumma mura'at al-ma'na thumma mura'at al-lafz*). Some claimed that what is in it is not as stated, because the pronoun in "abiding" does not refer to *man* as the pronouns before it do; rather it refers to the object of "He will admit," and "abiding" is a circumstantial clause of it, and its governing element is "He will admit," not the conditional verb. And this, as you see, is weak.
