Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 65, verse 12 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Allah is He who created seven heavens﴾ is a subject and predicate. ﴿And of the earth, the like of them﴾: that is, He created of the earth the like of them. Here *mithlahunna* ("the like of them") is the object of a verb that is elided, and the clause is coordinated with the clause before it. It has also been said that *mithlahunna* is coordinated with *sab' samawat* ("seven heavens"), and this is the view of al-Zamakhshari. On this view there is a separation by a prepositional phrase between the coordinating particle and the coordinated noun, which Abu Ali al-Farisi held to be restricted to poetic necessity. Al-Mufaddal transmitted from Asim, and Isma transmitted from Abu Bakr, the reading *mithluhunna* with a nominative (*raf'*) on the basis of its being the subject, with ﴿and of the earth﴾ as the predicate.

Likeness (*mithliyya*) can be realized through sharing some attributes. The majority (*jumhur*) said: the likeness here consists in their being seven, and in their being layered, one above another, with a distance between each earth and the next just as there is a distance between the heaven and the earth, and in each earth there are inhabitants of the creation of Allah, whose reality none knows but Allah the Exalted. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that they are either angels or jinn. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* and *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* related, through the route of Abu al-Duha,
[p. 144]
from him, that he said regarding the verse: "There are seven earths; in each earth is a prophet like your prophet, and Adam like Adam, and Nuh like Nuh, and Ibrahim like Ibrahim, and Isa like Isa." Al-Dhahabi said: its chain is sound, but it is anomalous in the extreme; I know of no one who follows Abu al-Duha in it. Abu Hayyan in *al-Bahr* mentioned something similar from the rabbi (*al-Habr*) and said: this is a hadith about whose fabrication there is no doubt, and it is from the narration of al-Waqidi, the liar.

I say: there is no rational or legal impediment to its being sound. What is meant is that in each earth there are creatures who trace back to a single origin, just as the descendants of Adam in our earth trace back to Adam, peace be upon him, and among them are individuals distinguished above the rest, like Nuh and Ibrahim and others among us.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, related from Ibn Umar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Between each earth and the one next to it is five hundred years. The highest of them rests on the back of a fish, whose two sides have met in the heaven; the fish is upon a rock, and the rock is in the hand of an angel. The second is the prison of the wind. The third contains the stones of Hell. The fourth contains its sulphur. The fifth contains its serpents. The sixth contains its scorpions. The seventh contains Saqar, and in it is Iblis, shackled with iron, one hand before him and one hand behind him, whom Allah the Exalted releases for whomever He wills." It is a *munkar* hadith, as al-Dhahabi said, and it is not to be relied upon at all. So do not be deceived by al-Hakim's grading of it. Similar reports on this subject are numerous; were it not for fear of tedium, we would have mentioned them to you. However, that the distance between each two earths is five hundred years, just as the distance between each two heavens is, has come in reports regarded as reliable, as related by Imam Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi from Abu Hurayra, who said: "While the Prophet (ﷺ) was sitting with his companions, he said: 'Do you know what is above you?' They said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It is the Raqi', a roof well-guarded and a wave held back.' He said: 'Do you know what is between you and it?' They said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'Between you and it is five hundred years.' Then he said: 'Do you know what is above that?' They said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'A heaven, and the distance between it and the one before is five hundred years.' Then he said likewise until he counted seven heavens, the distance between each two heavens being the distance between the heaven and the earth. Then he said: 'Do you know what is above that?' They said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'Above that is the Throne, and between it and the heaven is the distance between two heavens.' Then he said: 'Do you know what is beneath you?' They said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It is the earth.' Then he said: 'Do you know what is beneath that?' They said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'Beneath it is another earth, and between them is a journey of five hundred years,' until he (ﷺ) counted seven earths, the distance between each two earths being five hundred years."

The reports on measuring the distance between each two heavens in this manner are more numerous than those measuring it between each two earths, and more sound. Among them is what is mentioned in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and others of the sound collections. There is also in them that the thickness of each heaven is five hundred years. Therefore al-Razi's statement that this is not regarded as reliable by the people of verification is a claim whose offensiveness will not be hidden from anyone who has taken the most upright path of the Sunna. Yes, what he related, that the first heaven is a held-back wave, the second is rock, the third is iron, the fourth is copper, the fifth is silver, the sixth is gold, and the seventh is ruby, is not reliable at all, and no sound report has come with this detail. But his saying that it is something the intellect rejects, if he meant by it the denial of its possibility by reason, is an obvious prohibition.

Al-Dahhak said: they are seven in the sense that some are above others, not in the sense that they are so with a distance between one earth and another. Some scholars chose this, claiming that what is meant by those seven is the pure layer of soil adjacent to the center, the clay layer, the mineral layer in which minerals form, the layer mixed with other things and exposed, which is the dwelling of humankind and similar animals and in which plants grow, the layer of vapors, the frigid layer, and the layer of very fine breeze. It is not hidden that this is most like delirium. Similar to it is what some of those who examine the books of the sciences called "the New Wisdom" (*al-Hikma al-Jadida*, modern science) claim: that the earth separated from some of the heavenly bodies, becoming small, and then a layer formed above it, and so on until the whole became seven. He claimed that they had witnessed between each layer and the next traces of various creatures.

Abu Salih said: they are seven in number only, so they are seven flat earths, none above another, separated by seas, and the heaven overshadows all of them. This is also reported from Ibn Abbas. On this view, the relation between one earth and another is like the relation of America to Asia or Europe or Africa. But it has been said that those separating seas cannot be crossed.

It has also been said that they are among the seven climes, which differ in heat and cold, night and day, and other matters. Some have chosen this, but I do not think it is anything, because what is obvious is the consideration of a real separation of one earth from another in respect of likeness. It has been said that likeness is in creation, not in number or otherwise; so they are one earth, created like the seven heavens. This was supported by the fact that the earth is not mentioned in the Qur'an except in the singular. It was answered that it is sound, from the narration of al-Bukhari and others, that the Prophet said: "O Allah, Lord of the seven heavens and what they shade, and Lord of the seven earths and what they carry," the hadith in full. Likewise it is sound: "Whoever seizes a span of earth unjustly, it will be collared upon him from seven earths." The soundest of the views, as al-Qurtubi said, is the view of the majority mentioned above. On this basis, there is disagreement regarding whether the inhabitants of the earths other than this one see the heaven and derive light from it. It has been said that they see the heaven from every side of their earth and draw light from it.

It has also been said that they do not see the heaven, and that Allah the Exalted created for them a light which they see. The Imamiyya transmitted from some of the imams something similar to what the majority said. Al-Ayyashi related with his chain from al-Husayn ibn Khalid, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "He spread out his left palm, then placed his right upon it, and said: 'This is the lower earth, and the lower heaven is above it as a dome. The second earth is above the lower heaven, and the second heaven is above it as a dome. The third earth is above the second heaven, and the third heaven is above it as a dome,' until he mentioned the fourth, fifth, and sixth, and then said: 'The seventh earth is above the sixth heaven, and the seventh heaven is above it as a dome, and the Throne of the All-Merciful is above the seventh heaven.'" This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿seven heavens, and of the earth the like of them﴾, etc.

I say, in agreement with the majority's view, hoping for protection from the One upon whose axis of will the orbits of affairs revolve: they are seven earths, and between each earth and the next there is a great distance. In each earth there is a creation whose reality none knows but Allah the Exalted, and they have a light by which they are illuminated. It is possible that they have night and day, and it is not necessary that their light be from this sun or from this moon. It has come to predominate in the assumption of most people of the New Wisdom that the moon is a world like this earth of ours, with mountains and seas in it, and they claim that they perceive these through their observatories, and they are busy striving to verify the matter concerning it. So let what we say about the earths be on this model. They have also said: this sun, in a world, is the center of a circle, and its domain (*Bilqis*, here meaning its realm) is such that all its planets revolve around it in a specific manner and a regulated pattern, and some of the comets with tails, which they consider very numerous and which move in an egg-shaped orbit, draw near to it and withdraw from it to a limit that none knows but Allah the Exalted. They also think that the sun with its world is one of the satellites of another star, revolving around it as its satellites revolve around it. It is, from what we hear, one of the stars of the Najm (a star cluster). They have an assumption that this too is a satellite of another star, and so on. The great dominion of Allah the Exalted is vast; the realm of thought cannot encompass it, and the bounds of enumeration cannot contain it. The heaven of each world, as they consider it, is like the moon: it is that which its air reaches, until that body is in a sort of void in which nothing opposes it or weakens its motion. A body that moves in a void does not come to rest, since there is no opposition. So let each of these earths be borne by the hand of power between each two heavens, in the manner you heard from al-Rida, from his fathers, peace be upon them. And there is something by which its inhabitants are illuminated, floating in the sea of the power of Allah the Exalted. The relation of each earth to its heaven is that of a ring to a desert, and likewise the relation of the heaven to the heaven above it. It is possible that the earths, and likewise the heavens, are more than seven. The restriction to the stated number, which is a complete number, does not require the negation of more, for they have stated that a number has no implicit restriction (*mafhum*). The lowest heaven is the limit of the sphere in which the highest of the planets moves, and between it and this earth is a great distance.

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 65, verse 12 (part 2 of 2):

The Prophet's statement (ﷺ): "five hundred years" is by way of bringing the matter closer to people's understanding (al-taqrib li'l-afham). The matter becomes closer still if it is considered in relation to a rider who travels swiftly, as occurs in many reports that include a measurement of distance. And his statement (peace and blessings be upon him): "In the lowest heaven: 'a restrained wave' (mawj makfuf)" may be a eloquent metaphor (tashbih baligh) for fineness and the like, or it may be taken in its literal sense, with the tanwin in it indicating a type (li'l-nau'iyyah), until sound rational proof establishes its impossibility. The adorning of this heaven with the stars is because they appear in it as is observed, so it does no harm to this that they are all, or some, above it or below it. No proof has been established that any of the stars is fixed in any of the heavens like a gem in a ring or a nail in a board. Rather, some reports indicate the opposite. Yes, most reports concerning the heavens, the earth and the stars cannot be relied upon, as al-Nasafi indicated in Bahr al-kalam, and likewise what the early astronomers (qudama' ahl al-hay'ah) and their later successors have said. In each of what the two groups have held there is what agrees with our principles, what contradicts them, and what our Sharia is silent about, neither negating nor affirming it. Since it is among our principles that whenever rational proof conflicts with transmitted proof, the transmitted proof must be interpreted in light of the rational proof, because the rational proof is its foundation, and if it were invalidated by it, its own invalidity would follow. So the matter is easy, for the door of interpretation (ta'wil) is wider than the sphere of the fixed stars. I see no harm in interpreting some apparent meanings that are far-fetched by something that is not far-fetched, even if the far-fetchedness does not reach the level of impossibility, since that includes a religious benefit and does not entail contradicting something known of the religion by necessity. It may also be preferable to retain the apparent meaning and to commit the matter to the power of God, Exalted, which nothing can thwart, out of consideration for the minds of the common people who are bound to apparent meanings, and who regard departure from them—especially toward what agrees with the new wisdom (al-hikmah al-jadidah)—as sheer misguidance and pure disbelief. May God have mercy on a person who keeps speculation (al-ghaybah) away from himself.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Dari's and Ibn Jarir reported through the route of Mujahid from Ibn Abbas regarding this verse that he said: "If I were to tell you its interpretation, you would disbelieve, by denying it." In sum, whoever affirms the vastness of God's dominion and the greatness of His power, Mighty and Majestic, should not hesitate about the existence of seven earths in the manner we have mentioned. The seven may be understood as climes (al-aqalim) or as metallic and clay strata and the like, as previously mentioned. There is nothing in this that contradicts a necessary matter of religion or opposes a definitive proof from the evidences of the Muslims. Perhaps this plurality is what is most immediately understood from the verse, and what the reports demand. Nevertheless, it is not among the necessities of religion, so one who denies it or who wavers about it is not declared a disbeliever. Yet I see this only as coming from ignorance of what is most fitting to God's power and most worthy of His greatness. And God is the Granter of success to what is correct.

"The command descends among them" (yatanazzalu al-amru baynahunna): that is, the command of God, His decree and His destiny, Mighty and Majestic, proceeds among them, and His dominion takes effect within them. Ibn al-Mundhir and others reported from Qatadah that he said: "In every heaven and in every earth there is a creation of His, and a command of His, and a decree of His, Mighty and Majestic." It was also said: "The command descends among them" refers to life and death, wealth and poverty. It was also said: it is what He, Glorified, arranges within them of His wondrous arrangement, exalted is His majesty. Muqatil and others said: "the command" here means revelation, and "among them" indicates the space between this earth, which is the nearest of them, and the seventh heaven. Most scholars hold that it is decree and destiny, as previously stated, and that "among them" indicates the space between the lowest earth, which is the farthest of them, and the seventh heaven, which is the highest of them.

ʿĪsā and Abū ʿAmr in one narration read "yunazzilu" (the present tense of nazzala with doubling), with "al-amra" in the accusative, meaning: God causes the command to descend. "So that you may know that God is capable of all things" (li-ta'lamu anna Allaha 'ala kulli shay'in qadir): this is connected either to "khalaqa," or to "yatanazzalu," or to a implied element encompassing both, meaning: He did that so that you may know that whoever is capable of what has been mentioned is capable of all things. It was also said: the sense is "I have informed you of that so that you may know." It was read "liya'lamu" with the third-person ya' (yā' al-ghaybah).

"And that God has encompassed all things in knowledge" (wa-anna Allaha qad ahata bi-kulli shay'in 'ilma): because it is impossible for these acts to proceed from one who is not so.
